svg.text: The article runs as one spine from what silk is, through its properties and natural uses, to how humans try to
copy and then apply it — with the properties section fanning out into several measured traits that reconverge, and
the artificial-synthesis section splitting into the two separate problems (protein and apparatus) that engineers…

g.text: From spider biology to human use
Down the page follows the article's own order: what silk does for spiders, how it's built and performs, where it's used
in nature, the gland types behind it, how spiders spin it, then how people try to copy and finally apply it.

g.title: Silk serves many functions — Spiders use silk for traps, restraint, signalling, nests, flight, and even food. — → spya-gp4t9x
Properties: strength, toughness, stickiness — A hierarchical molecular structure gives silk its mechanical and adhesive traits. — → spya-py9zw6
Hard crystals, stretchy matrix — → spya-p263u9
Strong, stretchy, tough fibres — → spya-b0sewq
Glue-like attachment discs — → spya-m8z9e7
Silk used for prey capture, nests, courtship — → spya-rty5kb

g.title: Spun on demand, not grown — Silk is pulled from glands as a liquid-to-solid phase change, not continuously grown. — → spya-g3h8qq

g.text: Properties: one structure, several measured traits
A hub-and-satellite picture: the layered molecular structure is a single central idea, and the measured traits
(stiffness, strength, toughness, stretchiness under water, stickiness) are separate elaborations of it, not a sequence

g.title: Structure shapes mechanical traits — Crystalline beta-sheets plus an elastic amorphous matrix explain all the traits below. — → spya-py9zw6
Hard crystals, stretchy matrix — Alanine blocks form crystalline sheets; glycine-rich regions form the flexible matrix between them. — → spya-p263u9
Stiffness: Young's modulus — Spider silk is far more elastic than steel or Kevlar, which are stiffer but less yielding. — → spya-dq9b7q
Tensile strength rivals steel — Comparable to high-grade alloy steel, about half as strong as Kevlar fibres. — → spya-mhe2r5
Toughness beats Kevlar — The combination of strength and stretch lets silk absorb more energy before breaking than aramid fibres. — → spya-gfykz5
Water causes supercontraction — Wet dragline silk can shrink by half in length and behave like a weak rubber. — → spya-qdjb0x
Glue-like attachment discs — A separate adhesive secretion that sets instantly and stays usable indefinitely. — → spya-k8bh7d

g.text: A fork into two independent requirements — copying the protein and copying the spinning apparatus — each pursued by its
own methods, which then come back together in today's still-imperfect synthetic silks; a side branch shows the
apparatus work also enables non-fibre products.

g.title: Two tasks: protein + apparatus — Making artificial silk needs both the right unspun protein feedstock and a way to spin it. — → spya-wgee6t
Feedstock: copy the silk protein — → spya-rw0wtg
Geometry: copy the spinning duct — → spya-x4bwhf
Drawn from E. coli, silkworms, goats — Each source yields fibres with different strength and stretch, none matching nature exactly. — → spya-gjan3e
g.text: Drawn from E. coli, silkworms, goats

g.title: Syringes, microfluidics, electrospinning — Methods of varying cost and control for pulling or pushing the protein into a fibre. — → spya-up6vkg
Also: capsules, nanowires, membranes — The same apparatus work enables non-fibre forms, for drug delivery and tissue scaffolds. — → spya-r4r9au
Engineered silk: commercial, still weaker — Thicker, simpler, and less strong than natural dragline silk, but now sold commercially. — → spya-j7hems
